issues.contract_item: "(3) whether PerServiceCharges such as static IP are provisioned on this product, and which non-access component set was used ... Where any of these is unknown or contested, the assumption must be stated, its effect on the verdict shown, and the recommendation marked PROVISIONAL rather than certified."
issues.evidence_from_original: product-economics.md COS floor: 'R185 @ 100 users' (BNG R30.30 + Transit R28 + Backhaul R86 + Support R30 + BSS R11); vs Tarana all-in component list 'Wholesale + Static IP (R50) + BNG (R30) + Backhaul (R28) + BSS (R11) + Support (R10) + Install amortization (R213/12mo)' — non-access sum R129 vs R185.
issues.why_it_matters: The disclosure rule lets an implementation CHOOSE the lenient non-access stack (R129) over the COS-floor stack (R185), declare the choice, and pass. That is a R56/month swing which flips real verdicts. Worked case: 10% discount on the R1,299 entry tier gives effective revenue R1,169.10; lean basis 499+129+212.50 = R840.50 -> 28.1% (PASS, marginal band); COS-floor basis 499+185+212.50 = R896.50 -> 23.3% (BREACH of the 25% floor). The contract's own rank-1 quality says an understated cost basis means 'the gate can never fire' — yet the contract hands the implementation the lever to understate it legally. Declaring an assumption is made sufficient to pass a wrong answer.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace with: 'Where the source supports more than one non-access component set or leaves per-service provisioning unresolved, the HIGHEST-cost defensible basis must be used for the pass/fail verdict. Lower-cost readings may be shown alongside as sensitivity, never as the certified figure. The recommendation is marked PROVISIONAL and the ambiguity escalated. A verdict that passes only under the leniently-chosen basis must be reported as a breach.'

issues.contract_item: "The robust, assumption-independent conclusion — which is what the invariant enforces — is that the offer lands in or below the 25–35% marginal band ... The correct pairing is R1,899 ↔ R699."
issues.evidence_from_original: SKILL.md and references/pricing-guardrails.md both label R1,899 as 'SkyFibre SMB 50/25'; references/competitor-playbook.md Business Fibre benchmark table labels it 'CircleTel SkyFibre ... R1,899/mo (100)'; product-economics.md pairs R1,899 with the 200/50 tier at R699 wholesale.
issues.why_it_matters: The original's own document set assigns THREE different speeds to R1,899, which under product-economics map to R499, R599 and R699 wholesale. The contract silently resolves this by fiat and then declares the resulting conclusion 'assumption-independent'. It is not. At R599: cost = 599 + 185 + 212.50 = R996.50; effective revenue R1,582.50; margin = 37.0% — which is in the >=35% healthy/auto-approved band and directly contradicts the contract's stated conclusion that the offer 'is NOT auto-approvable'. The contract elsewhere insists the retail/wholesale pairing must be disclosed as an assumption; here it exempts itself from its own rule at the exact point a judge is most likely to use the number as an answer key.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace the decision text with: 'R1,899 is assigned three different speed labels across the source set (50/25, 100, 200/50), mapping to R499, R599 and R699 wholesale. The conservative pairing (R699) is used for the verdict and the ambiguity is escalated. The conclusion is NOT assumption-independent: at R599 the same offer computes 37.0% and would be auto-approvable. What is robust is only that the original's 88.9% is unattainable under every pairing.'

issues.contract_item: "A 20% discount on the entry tier breaches the 25% margin floor under EVERY defensible cost reading (21.4% on the published all-in, 13.7% itemised without static IP, 8.9% with) ... That the breach survives all three cost readings makes it the single most checkable and most damaging finding in the whole review."
issues.evidence_from_original: references/pricing-guardrails.md publishes 20% as a maximum on exactly one package — 'AirLink FWA 50/25 | R999 | R799 | 20%'. AirLink FWA's access is listed as 'Reyee 5GHz' (own infrastructure); product-economics.md publishes no wholesale MRC for it. SkyFibre SMB maxima are 16/17/18/18%; no R1,299 package appears in any max-discount table.
issues.why_it_matters: The three figures are arithmetically correct but computed on a package/discount pairing that does not exist in the original: they apply the Tarana entry tier's R1,299 retail, R499 wholesale and R817 all-in to a 20% maximum published only on an own-infrastructure AirLink package. Recomputed on the package where 20% is actually published: (R799 - R185 shared platform) / R799 = 76.8%, no breach. Recomputed on the package where the entry Tarana price lives, no 20% maximum is published at all. This is precisely the error the contract's own never_do forbids: 'Never invent, round up, or borrow a cost input from an unrelated product or a mismatched speed tier.' Elevating a constructed scenario to 'the single most checkable and most damaging finding' poisons any judge who treats it as ground truth.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace with: 'The published per-package maxima must each be re-tested against the corrected basis on the package they actually apply to, and the pairing stated. Where a maximum is published on an own-infrastructure product with no wholesale access line, the access component is R0 and must be shown as such, not borrowed from a wholesale-access product. The verified, in-source breach is the AUTHORITY breach: every published maximum of 15-20% requires managing director AND CFO, strategic accounts only, maximum 6 months, which the capability presents as routine.'

issues.contract_item: "Never compute or certify a margin on a cost basis that omits the per-customer wholesale access cost."
issues.evidence_from_original: references/pricing-guardrails.md 'COS by Product Line': AirLink FWA access is 'Reyee 5GHz', ParkConnect DUNE is 'Peraso 60GHz' — owned equipment, no wholesale line. product-economics.md 'Arlan MTN (Reseller): Wholesale R0 (commission model)'.
issues.why_it_matters: Stated as an absolute never_do it misfires on at least three of the capability's product lines. An implementation that correctly prices AirLink FWA or ParkConnect (no wholesale access exists) or an Arlan reseller deal (wholesale is R0 by construction) would be scored as violating a hard rule while being right. Constraint 78 acknowledges channel differences but the never_do overrides it, and never_do items are what get checked.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace with: 'Never compute or certify a margin on a cost basis that omits the per-customer access cost of the supply channel actually used. Where the channel carries no wholesale access charge (owned-infrastructure or commission-model products), that must be stated explicitly and the substituted cost basis — owned-equipment amortisation, or markup-plus-commission economics — shown in its place. Silence about access is the violation, not a zero.'

issues.contract_item: Three coexisting rules: never_do "Never approve, endorse or present as acceptable an offer whose correctly-computed margin is below the floor, regardless of strategic argument"; invariant "Minimum gross margin is 25% on all products, waivable only by written managing-director approval"; invariant "below 25% requires CFO approval and is rarely granted".
issues.evidence_from_original: margin-guardrails.md itself carries both '25% gross margin on ALL products — no exceptions without MD written approval' and a table row 'Low | < 25% | CFO approval (rarely granted)'.
issues.why_it_matters: The contract inherits a source contradiction and propagates all three versions without reconciling, then makes one of them absolute. An implementation that routes a 23%-margin offer to CFO (obeying invariant 135) violates the never_do; one that refuses outright violates invariants 134 and 135; one that routes to MD violates the other two. There is no compliant behaviour. This is a governance gate the contract ranks 5th in importance and cannot be satisfied as written.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace all three with one rule: 'Below 25% the capability must refuse to certify and must not present the offer as acceptable. It may state that the governing rules describe a written waiver route (managing director per the narrative rule, CFO per the threshold table — the two disagree at source and the conflict must be surfaced, not silently picked). Below 20% is never permitted under any authority.' Add the source conflict to open_questions_for_user.

issues.contract_item: "The SPECIFIC 2-hour figure is NOT asserted as a governing number ... The 2-hour figure appears in no governing rules file, so it is treated as a business decision rather than an invariant." / open question: "What maximum first-response time is the business committing to?"
issues.evidence_from_original: memory-os/long-term/mistakes.md, 2026-05-24 entry, Prevention: 'NEVER launch a campaign without: (a) confirmed product availability in the target geography, (b) a dedicated person handling leads within 2 hours, (c) conversion tracking from day one.'
issues.why_it_matters: The 2-hour standard is already a recorded business decision in a file CLAUDE.md makes a mandatory session-start read. The contract adopted clauses (a) and (c) from that same sentence as hard invariants — availability confirmation and day-one conversion tracking — and demoted clause (b) to an open question on a stated ground ('appears in no governing rules file') that applies identically to the two it kept. The result is an unstaffable invariant: response time must be 'stated' but no standard exists to state, and the user is asked a question already answered.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace the decision with: 'The recorded standard is a first response within 2 hours by a named person (memory-os/long-term/mistakes.md, 2026-05-24 Prevention). This is adopted as the default maximum first-response time; expected response volume must fit inside that standard at the named owner's capacity or the campaign is over-scoped.' Delete the corresponding open question or narrow it to the named-backup case.

issues.contract_item: No item anywhere in the contract names the published 'Min Price (25% margin)' column as below wholesale.
issues.evidence_from_original: SKILL.md Pricing Guardrails: 'SkyFibre SMB | R175.43 | Min Price (25% margin) R234'; 'BizFibreConnect | ~R150 | R200'; 'AirLink FWA | ~R100 | R133'. product-economics.md: Tarana wholesale R499-R699/customer/mo; DFA wholesale R650-R1,200/mo.
issues.why_it_matters: This is the most checkable and most catastrophic error in the original and the contract never names it. R234 is R265 BELOW the cheapest Tarana wholesale rate; R200 is R450 below the cheapest DFA rate; R133 is below the R185 shared platform floor that applies to every subscriber regardless of product. These are published as SAFE FLOORS, so a salesperson honouring them sells at a guaranteed cash loss on every unit. The contract's never_do bans the behaviour generically, but the audit trail that would let a judge verify the correction was actually made is absent — while three pages are spent on a constructed 20% scenario (A3) that is not in the source. Also unflagged: the per-product COS figures ~R150 and ~R100 are arithmetically impossible, being below the R185 shared platform minimum.
issues.recommended_fix: Add to unresolved_or_decided: 'The published Min Price (25% margin) column is invalid throughout. R234 (SkyFibre SMB) sits R265 below the cheapest Tarana wholesale MRC of R499; R200 (BizFibreConnect) sits R450 below the cheapest DFA wholesale of R650; R133 (AirLink FWA) sits below the R185 shared platform floor. The per-product COS figures of ~R150 and ~R100 are likewise below that floor and cannot be correct. The column must be withdrawn, not corrected in place.' Add the withdrawal to open_questions_for_user.

issues.contract_item: "Extractor 1 computed 35.7% ... Extractor 3's 64.5% is REJECTED"; "Extractor 1 is adopted"; "Extractor 1's scope boundary is correct about operating the funnel and wrong about planning for it." (10 occurrences across unresolved_or_decided)
issues.evidence_from_original: No equivalent in the original; this is contract-internal provenance metadata.
issues.why_it_matters: The block names three candidate positions, attributes each to a numbered source, and declares winners. A judge with sight of this can identify which implementation corresponds to which extractor from its characteristic figures (64.5%, R175.43 base, 2-hour/100%-contact invariants, portfolio percentages) and score by provenance rather than by output quality. 'Extractor 1 is adopted' is a direct instruction on which style wins.
issues.recommended_fix: Strip all extractor attributions. State each decision and its reasoning without provenance: e.g. 'Decision: the corrected margin lands in the 25-35% band under the conservative pairing. Reasoning: ...'. Keep the substance, delete every 'Extractor N' reference and every 'is adopted' / 'is REJECTED' verdict about a source.

issues.contract_item: "Point estimates: R1,017 published all-in → 35.7%; itemised at the 100-subscriber COS-floor tier without static IP → 30.7%; with static IP → 27.5%." and "True entry-tier discount headroom to the 25% floor is 16.1% / 7.9% / 2.8% across the three readings."
issues.evidence_from_original: The contract itself states the underlying component set is 'Recorded as an open ambiguity in the source, not resolved by fiat' and escalates it to the user.
issues.why_it_matters: All six figures verify arithmetically, but publishing them as point estimates over an ambiguity the contract declares unresolved turns them into an answer key. An implementation that derives a differently-but-validly-decomposed basis — or that correctly refuses to produce a point estimate given the ambiguity, which is what the contract's own assumption rule implies — scores worse than one that memorises 35.7/30.7/27.5. This implicitly favours one arithmetic presentation style over an equally defensible one.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace point estimates with the checkable band and the method: 'Under every defensible reading the corrected margin falls in the 27%-36% range against a claimed 88.9%; the specific figure depends on the unresolved component set and speed-tier pairing, both of which must be disclosed. Scoring should test whether access wholesale and amortised subsidies are present in the basis and whether the stated assumptions are named — not whether a particular decimal is reproduced.'

issues.contract_item: "Cash payback period = total campaign cash outlay ÷ expected new monthly gross profit from the campaign. This must be stated and must be shorter than the horizon the business can fund."
issues.evidence_from_original: CLAUDE.md Strategic Context: 'Cash: R86K (13 days runway)'. No fundable-horizon figure exists in the original or the governing rules.
issues.why_it_matters: The second clause is not checkable: 'the horizon the business can fund' is nowhere defined. Read literally against 13 days of runway, essentially no promotion with a monthly-recurring payback qualifies, so the gate is either vacuous or refuses everything. A judge cannot score it either way, and the contract lists the promotional budget as an open question while making this a hard invariant.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace with: 'Cash payback period = total campaign cash outlay ÷ expected new monthly gross profit from the campaign. The figure must be stated. It must be compared against a user-supplied fundable horizon; where that horizon has not been supplied, the payback figure must be stated, the missing input named, and the recommendation marked PROVISIONAL rather than passed or failed.'

issues.contract_item: "Never forecast results against generic benchmarks; forecast against this business's own demonstrated follow-up and conversion performance."
issues.evidence_from_original: memory-os/long-term/mistakes.md: '30 leads, 0 conversions'. The contract's own open question 11: 'The only observed data point is zero conversions from 30 leads, which cannot be used as a planning rate, and generic benchmarks are explicitly prohibited.'
issues.why_it_matters: The contract prohibits both of the only two available forecasting methods and admits it in its own open questions without resolving it. Every implementation must either forecast (violating the never_do) or refuse to forecast (leaving a load-bearing field blank, which a different never_do prohibits: 'Never emit a plan whose load-bearing fields — ... target numbers ... — are left as unfilled placeholders'). Two hard rules make a third impossible to satisfy.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace with: 'Never present an unsourced or unlabelled conversion assumption as a forecast. Where the business has no usable observed conversion rate — the only run produced zero conversions from 30 leads — an external benchmark may be used provided it is named, sourced, dated, and accompanied by a downside case at the observed rate, with the forecast marked as an assumption rather than a projection.'

issues.contract_item: "Conversion tracking from first response through to paid customer must be operational on day one of the campaign; if the tracking for a claimed metric does not exist, it must be built first or the metric must not be claimed."
issues.evidence_from_original: mistakes.md Prevention clause (c) 'conversion tracking from day one'. Contract scope_out: 'Executing anything: sending, publishing, buying media, building pages, forms or tracking pixels, configuring billing or CRM records.'
issues.why_it_matters: The outcome the user needs is that no metric is claimed which cannot actually be measured. 'It must be built first' is a procedure, and it is one the contract explicitly places out of scope in the same document — the capability is barred from building tracking and simultaneously required to build it. As written the invariant is unsatisfiable and self-contradictory.
issues.recommended_fix: Replace with: 'No metric may be claimed unless the system that would measure it is named and confirmed to exist and be capturing on day one. Where it does not exist, the plan must say so, name the metric as unmeasurable, and either drop it or list building it as a prerequisite for someone else — the capability does not build it.'

issues.contract_item: "Two free months on a 12-month contract is a 16.7% effective discount; three free months on 12 is 25.0% and is above the hard ceiling, therefore approvable by no one."
issues.evidence_from_original: references/pricing-guardrails.md, 'MD Approval Required': 'Free months | 3+ months | Business case + margin calc'; and 'Contract Term Extensions': '12 months → 24 months | 3 free months (still profitable)'. margin-guardrails.md discount ladder is denominated in price-discount percentage, with no months conversion.
issues.why_it_matters: The conversion insight is sound and worth keeping, but the conclusion is a strengthening the governing rules do not support. No rule establishes that a free-month concession is the same instrument as a percentage price discount for authority purposes; margin-guardrails' ladder is about discounts off price. The contract converts an offer the original routes to MD-with-business-case into one 'approvable by no one', and by the same arithmetic would forbid the original's explicitly sanctioned 12->24 month extension with 3 free months. A hard prohibition manufactured from an unestablished equivalence is exactly the failure mode listed in the contract's own never_do ('Never state an approval authority, threshold, band or duration limit that does not match the governing rules').
issues.recommended_fix: Replace with: 'Every concession denominated in months, waived fees or free equipment must be converted to an effective percentage of committed-term revenue and that percentage stated alongside the offer (two free months on 12 = 16.7%; three on 12 = 25.0%; three on 24 = 12.5%). Whether the percentage-denominated authority ladder governs month-denominated concessions is not settled by the governing rules and must be escalated, not assumed.' Add to open_questions_for_user.

issues.contract_item: "The R175 rate is reserved for a 1,500+ subscriber base and may not be used below that scale." / "R185 (100-subscriber tier) is the correct default at current scale."
issues.evidence_from_original: product-economics.md COS floor table binds R175 to '1,500+ users'; but the Infrastructure Fixed Costs table in the same file states 'BNG Service (Tier 1) | Echo SP | R30.30/subscriber | Drops to R20.20 at 1,000+'. That file also carries fixed costs not in the COS floor at all: NNI CrossConnect R5,000/mo, CGNAT R1,250, IP Transit minimum R700.
issues.why_it_matters: Two points. First, the source contradicts itself on whether R20.20 begins at 1,000 or 1,500 subscribers; the contract states one side as a flat invariant while elsewhere being scrupulous about surfacing source conflicts. Second and more materially, the contract asserts R185 as the correct default while listing the actual subscriber count as an open question — and the business (~R35K/month revenue, ~R15K of it recurring) is almost certainly well below 100 subscribers, the lowest tier the table publishes. At ~10 subscribers the R6,950/month of fixed NNI, CGNAT and minimum-transit cost alone is ~R695 per subscriber. The contract therefore commits the same class of error it corrects: adopting a scale-assumed figure that flatters cost.
issues.recommended_fix: Amend to: 'The published tiers begin at 100 subscribers and the source disagrees on whether the lowest BNG rate begins at 1,000 or 1,500. R185 is the most conservative PUBLISHED tier and is used as a floor, but it is itself a 100-subscriber figure; below 100 subscribers the published table does not apply and the per-subscriber share of fixed infrastructure (NNI R5,000, CGNAT R1,250, minimum transit R700) must be computed from the actual base. Any use of a published tier must state the assumed subscriber count.'

issues.contract_item: "Any margin verdict must state, alongside the number, the four assumptions that determine it: (1) ... (2) ... (3) ... (4) ..." and "The plan must state a spend ceiling, a hard end date, a defined reversion mechanism with a responsible party, and at least one leading indicator with a threshold that triggers pausing."
issues.evidence_from_original: The original's equivalent is a checklist ('Margin Calculation Checklist') which the contract otherwise treats as droppable procedure.
issues.why_it_matters: A fixed four-item disclosure taxonomy and an 'at least one leading indicator' count are templates in outcome costume. The outcome is that a reader can reproduce and overrule the verdict; enumerating exactly four named assumption slots and a minimum indicator count rewards form-filling and penalises an implementation that discloses a fifth material assumption instead.
issues.recommended_fix: Rewrite as outcome: 'Any margin verdict must disclose every assumption that materially moves it, such that a third party can reproduce the number and see which input would change the verdict if wrong.' Keep the four as illustrative examples, not as a required enumeration. Replace 'at least one leading indicator with a threshold' with 'a stated condition under which the campaign is paused.'

issues.contract_item: "Resold/commission-channel products must retain at least their category markup floor (IoT/M2M 20%, Fleet 18%, Data/Backup/Mobile Workforce 15%, Voice 10%, Device Upgrade 8%, Venue WiFi 20%)" and "Volume discount schedule: 1–4 lines 0%; 5–9 lines 5%; 10–19 lines 8%; 20–49 lines 10%; 50+ lines 12%."
issues.evidence_from_original: The original skill's entire product set is SkyFibre SMB, BizFibreConnect, AirLink FWA, ParkConnect DUNE, CircleConnect LTE, ClinicConnect and Managed IT. Arlan/reseller products and per-line volume tiers appear nowhere in SKILL.md or any of its three reference files.
issues.why_it_matters: Both tables are real policy from margin-guardrails.md, so this is defensible import rather than fabrication — but they add checkable invariants for a channel the capability has never covered, expanding the surface a judge tests against beyond what the user's promotional-campaign work touches. Faithful to the rules file, unfaithful to the capability's scope.
issues.recommended_fix: Demote both from objective_invariants to constraints, conditioned: 'Where a promotion touches a resold/commission-channel product or a multi-line deal, the governing category markup floors and volume-discount schedule apply and must be sourced from the rules file rather than reproduced here.'

issues.contract_item: non_qualities: "Breadth of a forward campaign calendar — committing to future promotions whose affordability cannot be assessed today is not planning."
issues.evidence_from_original: SKILL.md 'Seasonal Campaign Calendar': Mar-Apr tax season, Aug-Sep back to school, Oct-Nov Black Friday, Dec retention focus — South-Africa-specific demand timing.
issues.why_it_matters: The reasoning for demoting a committed forward calendar is correct, but the demotion also discards knowledge of WHEN demand exists in this market, which is an outcome the user values (activation_expectations still fires on 'a seasonal, event-driven or launch-timed push' but nothing tells the capability which moments those are). Dropping the commitment is right; dropping the timing knowledge is an over-correction.
issues.recommended_fix: Amend the non_quality to: 'Breadth of a forward campaign CALENDAR OF COMMITMENTS ...' and add to scope_in: 'Identifying whether the requested timing coincides with a known local demand moment (tax season, back-to-school, Black Friday, December quiet period) and what that implies for the offer — without pre-committing to future promotions whose affordability cannot be assessed today.'

issues.contract_item: "Coverage Ratio = (qualifying subscribers × per-customer wholesale rate) ÷ minimum spend commitment"
issues.evidence_from_original: margin-guardrails.md: 'MSC Coverage Ratio = (Tarana Customers × R499) / MSC Commitment'.
issues.why_it_matters: The governing formula pins R499. The contract silently generalises to 'per-customer wholesale rate', which is arguably more correct given tiered wholesale — but it is a restatement of a governing formula presented as if it were the governing formula, and it changes the computed ratio for any customer not on the R499 tier. The contract's own never_do bars stating a threshold 'that does not match the governing rules'; the same standard should apply to formulas.
issues.recommended_fix: Amend to: 'Coverage Ratio = (qualifying subscribers × per-customer wholesale rate) ÷ minimum spend commitment. Note: the governing rule states this with R499 fixed; using the tier-matched rate is a deliberate correction and must be flagged as such when the ratio is reported.'

faithfulness_verdict: No — qualified. The contract is a substantial and largely correct improvement on the original: it correctly identifies that the original's whole margin apparatus is built on a cost basis that omits the single largest cost component, and its replacement formula, mandatory component list, margin bands, discount-authority ladder, volume schedule, bundle rules, term adjustments and MSC treatment are all faithful to the governing rules files, verbatim-accurate where they should be, and correctly separate gross-margin cost of sale from acquisition cost. Its capture of what the user actually needs is strong: the refusal-with-alternative behaviour, cash-versus-percentage distinction, deliverability precondition, conversion-handover, expiry and reversion, and the confidentiality firewall are all genuine outcomes rather than procedure, and the procedural material it drops (templates, segment taxonomies, competitor dossiers, mechanic rankings) is correctly dropped with reasoning. It is unfaithful in five specific ways. (1) Its assumption-disclosure rule is a loophole rather than a guard: an implementation may select the cheaper of two defensible non-access stacks, declare it, and pass an offer that breaches the floor under the other — defeating the contract's own rank-1 quality (A1). (2) It exempts itself from its own disclosure discipline at the flagship worked example, declaring a speed-tier pairing 'correct' and the resulting conclusion 'assumption-independent' when the original's own documents support two other pairings, one of which flips the verdict to auto-approvable (A2). (3) Its self-declared most important finding is computed on a package/discount pairing that does not exist in the source, by exactly the cost-borrowing its own never_do prohibits (A3). (4) It omits the most checkable error in the original entirely — published minimum prices sitting hundreds of rand below wholesale (A7). (5) Several hard rules are mutually unsatisfiable: the sub-25% routing rule contradicts itself three ways (A5), the forecasting prohibition rules out both available methods while another rule forbids leaving the field blank (A11), and the tracking invariant requires building what scope_out forbids building (A12). It also demotes an already-decided business standard (2-hour response) to an open question on grounds it does not apply to two sibling clauses it kept (A6).
would_rig_benchmark: Yes. Two concrete mechanisms. First, unresolved_or_decided names 'Extractor 1', 'Extractor 2' and 'Extractor 3' in ten places, attributes distinctive positions and figures to each (64.5%, R175.43 as base, a 2-hour first-response standard with a 100% contact target, the 20%/15% portfolio ceilings), and then declares winners — 'Extractor 1 is adopted', 'Extractor 3's 64.5% is REJECTED', 'Extractor 1's scope boundary is correct about operating the funnel and wrong about planning for it'. Any judge with sight of this can fingerprint an implementation by its characteristic numbers and score by provenance rather than output, and is told outright which lineage is preferred. Second, the contract publishes six precise point estimates (35.7% / 30.7% / 27.5%; 16.1% / 7.9% / 2.8%) plus 21.4/13.7/8.9 and 21.7% over an ambiguity it simultaneously declares 'recorded as an open ambiguity in the source, not resolved by fiat'. That converts a genuinely underdetermined calculation into an answer key: an implementation that correctly refuses a point estimate, or that decomposes the basis differently but validly, scores worse than one reproducing the decimals. The rigging is compounded by A3, because one of those keys is derived from a scenario absent from the source — an implementation that correctly declines to find a 20% breach on the Tarana entry tier would be marked wrong. Recommended remediation: delete all extractor attributions; replace point estimates with the verified band plus the method to be checked (is access wholesale in the basis, are subsidies amortised, is the speed-tier pairing disclosed, is the subscriber tier disclosed); and remove the A3 scenario.
arithmetic_verdict: INDEPENDENT DERIVATION (performed before reading the contract's answer). product-economics.md publishes a per-subscriber Cost of Sale Floor of BNG + IP Transit + Backhaul + Support + BSS totalling R185 at 100 users, R182 at 300, R179 at 1,000, R175 at 1,500+, with the explicit note 'Excludes access costs (Tarana/DFA wholesale) — add those per product.' The original skill's R175.43 is the same stack recomputed with BNG at R20.20, which pricing-guardrails.md itself labels 'Tier 4 volume rate (>1k users)'. Therefore the correct basis is: Total COS per subscriber per month = access wholesale MRC for the specific product AND speed tier (Tarana R499 / R599 / R699 for 50-12.5 / 100-25 / 200-50; DFA R650-R1,200) + shared platform COS at the actual subscriber-count tier + per-service charges where provisioned (static IP R50) + one-off subsidies amortised over the committed term (installation R2,550 / 12 = R212.50 per month). Marketing spend, commission and overhead sit outside gross margin. Any margin computed on the shared stack alone is invalid, and the original's is. CONTRACT MATCHES THIS DERIVATION EXACTLY — formula, mandatory component list, exclusions and amortisation. VERIFICATION OF THE CONTRACT'S FIGURES: all check. Reconciliation gap: R499+R50+R30+R28+R11+R10+R212.50 = R840.50 vs published R817 (gap R23.50), and identically R940.50 vs R917 and R1,040.50 vs R1,017 — the contract's R23.50 at all three tiers is correct. Flagship example, R1,899 with two free months on 12 months, effective revenue R1,582.50: against R1,017 published all-in, 35.73% (contract 35.7%, correct); against R699+R185+R212.50 = R1,096.50, 30.71% (contract 30.7%, correct); adding static IP R50, 27.55% (contract 27.5%, correct). Error versus the original's 88.9% is 53.2 to 61.4 points (contract '53-61', correct). Speed upgrade: entry tier R1,299 less R817 = 37.1%; upgrading access from R499 to R699 raises cost to R1,017 giving (1299-1017)/1299 = 21.71% (contract 21.7%, correct — and it is a floor breach). Approval bands, discount-authority ladder, volume schedule, bundle 30%/15%, term adjustments, Arlan markup floors: all verbatim faithful to margin-guardrails.md. SPECIFIC CLAIMS THE AUDIT WAS ASKED TO TEST. (i) 'The published cost floor is a high-volume rate not applicable at current scale' — CONFIRMED. R175.43 depends on BNG at R20.20, explicitly labelled a >1k-user volume rate, and product-economics binds R175 to a 1,500+ base. The business is at roughly R35K/month revenue with ~R15K recurring, so it is not merely below 1,500 but almost certainly below 100 — the lowest tier published. The contract is right that R175 is inadmissible, but it then adopts R185 as 'the correct default at current scale' while listing the subscriber count as an open question, and R185 is itself a 100-subscriber figure. At ~10 subscribers the fixed NNI (R5,000), CGNAT (R1,250) and minimum transit (R700) alone are ~R695 per subscriber. The contract is directionally right and still optimistic (see A14). It also states 'R175 may not be used below 1,500+' as settled when the same source file says the rate drops at 1,000+. (ii) 'Certain published minimum prices fall below wholesale' — CONFIRMED, and MORE SEVERELY THAN THE CONTRACT ACKNOWLEDGES. SkyFibre SMB's published Min Price of R234 is R265 below the cheapest Tarana wholesale rate of R499 and R465 below R699. BizFibreConnect's R200 is R450 below the cheapest DFA rate of R650 and R1,000 below R1,200. AirLink FWA's R133 is below the R185 shared platform floor that applies to every subscriber irrespective of product, as are the published per-product COS figures of ~R150 and ~R100. The contract bans the behaviour generically but never names this column, which is the single most checkable error in the original (A7). (iii) 'Is the assumption-disclosure rule sufficient?' — NO. It prevents silent error but not deliberate leniency. It expressly permits choosing between two non-access stacks that differ by R56 per subscriber per month (R129 lean versus R185 COS-floor), so a 10% discount on the R1,299 entry tier computes 28.1% (pass) on the lean basis and 23.3% (breach) on the COS-floor basis, and either verdict is contract-compliant provided the choice is declared. A rule that lets a breach be certified as a pass by declaration defeats the contract's own rank-1 quality (A1). The fix is to mandate the highest-cost defensible basis for the verdict and relegate lower-cost readings to sensitivity. OVERALL: the contract's formula, mandatory components, thresholds and approval bands are CORRECT and materially better than the original; every figure it publishes verifies. Its errors are not in the arithmetic but in the epistemics around it — an over-permissive disclosure rule, a fiat resolution of the speed-tier pairing dressed as assumption-independence, a flagship breach computed on a pairing absent from the source, and the omission of the below-wholesale minimum-price column.
